list.listitem: Maintain a high clinical suspicion for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) in patients who have rapidly progressive dementia with ataxia, new vision or sensory complaints, and/or psychiatric symptoms. C
Diagnostic tests that can be performed to assist in making a diagnosis include diffusion-weighted MRI, EEG, and CSF 14-3-3 and RT-QuIC assays. C
Treatment is primarily symptomatic and palliative. C

background.definition: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a progressively and universally fatal degenerative brain disorder caused by misfolded, infectious protein particle called a prion. CJD falls under a broader category of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs). All types of CJD are characterized by the accumulation of an insoluble prion protein (PrPsc) in the brain, which causes a variety of symptoms; typically including progressive motor, cognitive, and behavioral symptoms. There are at least 6 subtypes ().

list.listitem: Annual rate of diagnosis of CJD (all types) worldwide is 1-2 cases per million.
In the United States, only 300 cases of CJD are noted annually.
Variant CJD incidence peaked in 1999 and has been decreasing ever since, partly due to heightened screening measures.
Persons in United Kingdom are at greater risk for variant CJD.
There is no known cause of the most common type of CJD, sporadic CJD (sCJD).
Familial CJD is an inherited disorder. Studies have shown that there is a gene mutation of the PrPc gene. It is a dominant disorder that has almost 100% penetrance.

Variant CJD is, as noted above, an acquired disorder associated with bovine spongiform encephalopathy, acquired typically from ingestion of infected beef (but not milk products). It was first recognized in 1995 in the United Kingdom where the majority of cases have been to date. This disease is initiated by dietary or other exposure to bovine "prions" (PrPsc).

Iatrogenic CJD (iCJD) is associated with procedures such as corneal transplants, dura mater implantation, and other infected products. In general, iCJD is very rare and occurs as a result of accidental transmission by medical treatment.

CJD is a neurodegenerative disease caused by the mutation of the PRNP gene. This protein is altered from the normal PrPc to a PrPsc either by spontaneous mutation/activation of native PrPc or by direct infection with PrPsc depending on the type of CJD. These "prions" (PrPsc particles) accumulate in large numbers in brain tissue disrupting brain function.

The normal protein PrPc is used as a template for the PrPsc to replicate without the need for DNA. This is the cause of the rapid progression of the disease. Some research will classify this progression as abnormal protein folding leading to large aggregates of prions.

There are actually five subtypes of sCJD resulting from the possible combination of PrP gene polymorphisms. Codon 129 can encode for methionine or valine, thus a patient carries M/M, V/V, or M/V. The polymorphisms are a modifier of disease. There are also two types of PrPsc. This partially explains the variation of symptom presentation and progression.
In familial CJD, activation of "prion folding" occurs due to a genetic mutation specifically affecting the PRNP gene. E200K is a recognized mutation with can be detected.

Studies for pathophysiology of variant and iCJD have surmised that prions most likely travel through certain tissues in our immune system, particularly the lymph nodes and spleen, carrying the prion via HLAs (human leukocyte antigens) to the brain. In variant CJD, resulting prion aggregates form characteristic "daisy" or florid plaques.
Genetic screening and counseling are available for familial CJD but there is no current treatment. C
To avoid iCJD, medical instruments used on patients with confirmed CJD must be disposed of due to the inability to reliably remove prions from instrumentation. C
The United Kingdom has instituted a new policy for blood banks that reduces the risk of CJD transmission by leukocyte depletion techniques. C
Suspect CJD in patients with rapidly progressing dementia, especially if accompanied by new onset motor or visual disturbances and new psychiatric abnormalities. C
Presumptive diagnosis can be made clinically () and confirmed by identifying specific findings on diffusion-weighted MRI, EEG, and/or CSF analysis for 14-3-3 protein. C
RT-QulC is a relatively new CSF exam with very high sensitivity and specificity.
Definitive diagnosis can only be made at death with brain autopsy. C

list.listitem: See for diagnostic criteria.

In sCJD, the average age of presentation is 67 years and the most common presenting complaints are dementia, ataxia, and visual disturbances. During the course of disease, patients often develop myoclonus (90%), ataxia (59%), visual symptoms (52%), extrapyramidal signs (51%), and most die in a state of akinetic mutism. Median survival is approximately 3 months.

Nonspecific complaints such as anxiety, sleep disturbance, weight loss, and decreased appetite occur in about 25% of patients. Patients who present early may complain of paranoia and hallucinations. Most of these patients exhibit startle myoclonus.
If patients present late in the disease progression, they may have frank dementia then phase into a mute and akinetic state.
Patients with familial CJD usually present at an average age of 52 years; their symptoms depend on the specific gene mutation. The course of disease is somewhat longer than that of sCJD.

Patients with variant CJD typically present at an average age of 28 years with unpleasant sensory and psychiatric disturbances. Symptoms of ataxia and cognitive decline emerge and later in disease, chorea and myoclonus appear. See .

Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) MRI: Perform an MRI if CJD is clinically suspected. One study showed 92.3% sensitivity of detecting lesions and another of patients with familial CJD showed a sensitivity of 77% and a specificity of 100% with DWI abnormality in the caudate nucleus and a sensitivity of 87% and specificity of 91% of FLAIR signal intensity abnormality in the caudate or putamen nuclei. Up to 80% of patients with sCJD may have increased signaling shown in basal ganglia and deep cortical layers. Areas of increased signal correspond to spongiform change.
Finally, a systematic review of 15 studies with 1144 patients found an overall sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 97% (LR+ 30, LR- 0.09).
Wilson's disease and carbon monoxide poisoning can have similar findings.

EEG: Between 60% and 80% of patients with sCJD will have periodic sharp wave complexes. The EEG can also have slowing or burst wave suppression. EEGs in patients with variant CJD are much less likely to have these findings.
CSF test for 14-3-3 protein: Sensitivity of this test for sCJD is between 93% and 97%. This protein may also be present in patients with stroke, tumor, or viral encephalitis.

In one study, the sensitivities of CSF proteins 14-3-3, tau protein and S-100b, for sCJD were 96% to 98%. The sensitivity was greater for early diagnosis of sCJD (<6 weeks from symptom onset) compared with later diagnosis, and CSF tau protein had the greatest specificity (82%).

CSF real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) test has a sensitivity of 85.7% and specificity of 100%. There have been studies on using the RT-QulC on olfactory mucosa nasal brushing and they have been promising.
Firm diagnosis can only be made at autopsy via direct analysis of brain. Diagnosis is most accurate when autopsy is performed within 24 hours of death.
Care is symptomatic and palliative. C
A single RCT of 28 patients found that the analgesic flupirtine (Effirma) appears to slow the cognitive decline in patients with CJD but does not increase survival. B

Treatment of CJD is primarily symptomatic. A systematic review identified numerous case studies and case series but few clinical trials. Drugs studied included antivirals, antimalarials, antifungals, and anticonvulsants. A single RCT of 28 patients found that the analgesic flupirtine appears to slow the cognitive decline in patients with CJD but does not increase survival. Studies are ongoing to evaluate doxycycline and quinacrine.
Extrapyramidal symptoms can be treated with anti-Parkinson drugs.
Most patients will show signs of depression that can be treated with antidepressants.
Prognosis is poor; 90% die within a year due to complications usually associated with respiratory infections. C
Older patients are at the highest risk for familial CJD since the onset of the disease presents around the age of 50 years.
Recent studies have shown that people of Libyan Jewish decent are at a higher risk due to a common PRNP E200K mutation. Genetic testing in affected families is available.

Affects mainly people older than 50 years; ataxia, dementia spongiform change, rarely plaques; short course
-Includes familial CJD, Gerstmann-Straüssler-Scheinker Syndrome, and fatal familial
Often younger onset than sCJD; symptom pattern depends on type of mutation, but sometimes like sCJD; course illness is usually longer
Contamination through brain surgery, corneal transplant, dura mater graft, human growth hormone.
Age of onset depends on age at exposure and on incubation time; clinical and pathologic features often indistinguishable from sCJD
Young onset and longer duration than classical CJD; psychiatric signs at presentation; distinctive “daisy” plaques
